theme_intro: Depression pulls people away from each other at exactly the moment they need each other most. This week looks at what research says about connection: why withdrawing is a symptom rather than a failing, why belonging to groups protects against depression and relapse, and how the smallest step back towards people, one message or one shared room, counts. A faith community is one place to belong; choirs, classes, walking groups and support groups are others.

days.title: Pulling away is the illness talking
days.quote: Depression is an insidious, isolating disorder, which can sabotage relationships.
days.quote_source: Margarita Tartakovsky (2012), 9 Best Ways to Support Someone with Depression
days.explanation:
If you have stopped answering messages, cancelled plans, or let the phone ring out, you are not a bad friend. Withdrawal is one of the core symptoms of depression. Researchers who study the condition describe it as an illness "characterized by withdrawal, purposelessness and loneliness". The pulling away is not a decision you made. It is part of what depression does.

There is a loop here, and it helps to see it. Low energy and low motivation make contact feel like a mountain, so you stay in. Staying in removes the small good moments that other people bring and leaves more room for the mind to replay painful thoughts. Mood sinks further, and contact feels even harder. A self-help programme from the Centre for Clinical Interventions calls this the vicious cycle of depression, and it applies to people as much as to activities.

The loop runs the other way too, and that is the hopeful part. Large studies find that losing connection often comes before depression, and that regaining connection predicts recovery more strongly than depression predicts withdrawal. The World Health Organization's group therapy manual asks facilitators to explain exactly this: when depressed you may not feel like going out, but if you do go out you have a greater chance of feeling better. Nothing is required of you today except noticing. The withdrawal is the illness. You are still in there.
days.challenge: Today, only notice. Take two minutes and write down, in the journal or on paper, three names: someone you have been avoiding, someone who has tried to reach you, and someone you would like to hear from. Do not contact anyone yet. Notice what you feel when you write each name, without arguing with it. If three names is too much today, think of one person and hold them in mind for one slow breath. That counts.
reflection_questions: When did you last notice yourself pulling back from people? What was going on that week?
What does your mind say will happen if you reach out? How much of that is the illness speaking?
Who has kept gently knocking, even when you did not open the door?

scripture.text: Turn to me, and have mercy on me, for I am desolate and afflicted.

days.title: What five thousand people taught us
days.quote: Depressed respondents with no group memberships who joined one group reduced their risk of depression relapse by 24%; if they joined three groups their risk of relapse reduced by 63%.
days.quote_source: Cruwys, Dingle, Haslam, Haslam, Jetten & Morton (2013)
days.explanation:
In England, more than 5,000 adults over fifty have been interviewed every two years since 2002. Among many other questions, they are asked which organisations, clubs or societies they belong to: a church or religious group, a sports club or exercise class, a music group or evening class, a residents' association, a charity, a social club. A team of psychologists at the University of Queensland used these answers to ask a plain question: does belonging to groups change the course of depression?

It did. The more groups a person belonged to, the lower their depression two and four years later, even after taking into account age, health, income, relationship status and how depressed they were to begin with. The effect was strongest for people who had already been depressed. Among them, 41% of those who belonged to no groups had relapsed six years later, compared with 15% of those in three or more. The authors concluded that it is not "too late" to address isolation once depression has arrived.

A Korean study of about 6,600 people over sixty found something similar across three years: those who took part in a social activity at least once a week were less likely to become depressed, and those who combined two or three kinds of activity, social, religious or physical, had roughly a third lower risk. These are studies of older adults, and they observe rather than prove. But they point the same way. Groups are not a treatment on their own and not a replacement for one. They are one of the few protective factors you can actually join.
days.challenge: Take five minutes and list every group you belong to, or used to belong to, however loosely: a congregation, a team, a class, a chat group that sometimes meets in real life, colleagues who eat together, a family that gathers. Do not judge the list. Then put a small mark next to the one that would be easiest to be present in again. If listing feels too heavy, name one group out loud and leave it there for today.
reflection_questions: Which groups have you belonged to in your life, and which one did you miss most when it ended?
If one membership can change the odds, which one would be the least frightening to renew?
What stops you counting yourself as a member of a group you still technically belong to?

scripture.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn't have another to lift him up.

days.title: Belonging is more than showing up
days.quote: Most particularly, it suggests that tackling the challenge of depression involves not just putting the person back into the group, but also putting the group back into the person.
days.quote_source: Cruwys, Haslam, Dingle, Jetten, Hornsey, Chong & Oei (2014)
days.explanation:
After finding that group memberships protect against depression, the same researchers asked a sharper question: is it the attending that helps, or the belonging? They followed 52 people in a disadvantaged Australian city who had been referred to community recreation groups: indoor soccer, sewing, yoga, art. Three months later, how often someone had attended made no difference to their depression. What mattered was whether they felt part of the group. Among those who felt little belonging, about half still scored as depressed; among those who felt they belonged, under a third did.

They then repeated the study with 92 outpatients in group therapy at a psychiatric hospital. Same result. Attendance did not predict improvement; identifying with the group did, and it mattered more for depression than for anxiety. The researchers' term for this is social identification: the sense that this group is part of who I am, that these people are "us".

This is good news and hard news. The hard part is that belonging cannot be forced, and sitting in a room where you feel like an outsider will not do much. The good part is that fit matters more than effort, so it is worth choosing groups where you can be yourself. And belonging can begin quietly. The WHO group therapy manual describes a woman called Kayla who sat silent for weeks, until the others invited her to practise holiday songs with them. Her depression scores began to move after that. Acceptance has to be offered by others; your part is staying long enough to receive it.
days.challenge: Think back over your life for a moment when you felt like one of "us": a team, a class, a kitchen full of relatives, a youth group, a ward of other patients. Spend five minutes writing what made it feel that way: being greeted by name, having a role, shared jokes, being needed. Keep that list; it describes the kind of group worth looking for. If remembering is painful today, write down one person who once made you feel welcome, and stop there.
reflection_questions: Where in your life have you felt most clearly "one of us"? What did people there do that made it so?
Is there a group you attend without feeling you belong? What would need to change, in the group or in you, for that to shift?
Who would notice if you stopped coming?

scripture.text: So we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

days.title: The one-message day
days.quote: Although the coffee was not as good as he was used to, at least he was not alone that day.
days.quote_source: World Health Organization & Columbia University (2016), Group Interpersonal Therapy for Depression
days.explanation:
The WHO manual for group therapy tells the story of Ali, a 48-year-old man who had fled his country after his wife and sons were killed. In the new country he trusted no one. When members of his therapy group invited him out, he thanked them and refused, week after week. Eventually he went, mostly so as not to offend them. The coffee was poor. But he was not alone that day, and he said he felt a little better. The next week he went out again, met a man from his home village, and within a few weeks his depression had lifted.

Nobody is promising you Ali's ending. The point is the size of his first step. Behavioural activation, the approach behind most depression self-help, rests on one observation: when you are depressed, action has to come before motivation, because motivation does not arrive on its own. The same goes for people. You will not feel like sending the message. Send it anyway, and make it small enough that feeling is not required.

One caution about the medium. In a survey of over a thousand students, having more online-only contacts went with more depressive symptoms, while having more online contacts who were also real-life friends went with fewer. Scrolling is not contact. A message to one real person, someone you could in principle sit in a room with, is. It does not need to be honest about everything. It needs to exist.
days.challenge: Send one message to one real person today. Keep it tiny, so that it asks nothing of you or of them: "Thinking of you today. No need to reply." or "Saw this and thought of you." Choose someone from the names you wrote on day one. Press send before you have finished deciding whether to. If sending is too much, reply to a message you have been ignoring with a single word or a heart. If even that is too much, write the message and save it as a draft for tomorrow.
reflection_questions: What did your mind predict would happen when you sent the message? What actually happened?
Who is the person you would most like to hear from, unprompted, with no need to reply?
When you are well, what small contact do you make without thinking about it?

scripture.text: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

days.title: How to say "I am not okay"
days.quote: Often, problems seem bigger than they really are when a person tries to deal with them on their own.
days.quote_source: Centre for Clinical Interventions, Back from the Bluez, Module 9: Self-Management
days.explanation:
Telling someone that you are depressed can feel harder than being depressed. Shame says you will be a burden. Experience may say that people respond badly: with advice, with comparisons, with "it is all in your head". Deborah Serani, a psychologist who has lived with depression herself, lists exactly those responses as the ones that push people further into isolation. So the fear is not irrational. It is also not the whole story.

Sociologist Peggy Thoits, reviewing thirty years of research on social support, describes two things supporters give. One is emotional sustenance: being there, listening, sitting in companionate silence. The other is practical help: a lift, a meal, a phone call made on your behalf. She also notes that people who have been through the same thing offer something family often cannot, which is why a support group, or a friend who has had depression, may understand faster. You can choose who gets which conversation.

It helps to be specific. In a series of studies, people who first expressed gratitude to a friend became more comfortable raising concerns with that friend afterwards. So begin with thanks, then name the thing, then ask for one concrete action: "Thank you for sticking around. I have been struggling with depression for a while. I do not need you to fix it. It would help if you could check in on Wednesdays." And if the thing you have not been saying is that you have thoughts of ending your life, please say that too, today: to a crisis line (the Help page has your country's number) and to your doctor. That is the most important sentence in this whole week.
days.challenge: Choose one person and one sentence. Write the sentence first, in three parts: a thank you, the truth in one line, and one specific request (a weekly check-in, company at an appointment, a meal, a walk). Then say it today, out loud or in writing. If saying it is too much, write it in your journal and decide only who will receive it and when. If your truth includes thoughts of suicide, say it to a crisis line today; that is the one request that cannot wait.
reflection_questions: What do you fear will happen if you tell someone? Has that ever actually happened, and with whom?
Who in your life gives comfort well, and who gives practical help well? They may not be the same person.
What is one specific thing that would help this week, if someone offered it?

scripture.text: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

days.title: For the people who love you
days.quote: When I was struggling with my own depression, the most healing moments came when someone I loved simply sat with me while I cried, or wordlessly held my hand, or spoke warmly to me with statements like 'You're so important to me.' 'Tell me what I can do to help you.' 'We're going to find a way to help you to feel better.'
days.explanation:
This message is written to be forwarded. If you are depressed, send it to someone who wants to help and does not know how. If you are that someone, read on.

Deborah Serani, a psychologist who has had depression herself, offers nine things that help. Be there; presence matters more than words. Make small gestures: a text, a card, a cooked meal, a voicemail. Do not judge or criticise; telling someone it is all in their head implies they chose this. Do not try tough love or ultimatums; it is as useless and harmful as pushing away someone who has cancer. Do not minimise the pain or call them thin-skinned. Do not give advice; ask instead, "What can we do to help you feel better?" Do not compare it to your own low days. Learn about depression, especially that it ebbs and flows, so a good day is not the end of it. And be patient, because patience is what tells a depressed person you will still be there however long it takes.

Research on social support backs this up. Peggy Thoits describes the help that close family and friends give best as emotional sustenance: showing you understand what this means for the person, listening to their worries, keeping them company in silence or in ordinary activity, and quietly helping with practical tasks. If you are the one who is depressed: you are allowed to tell people which of these you need. Point at this list. Letting someone support you well is itself a step back towards connection.
days.challenge: Forward this message, or copy two or three lines from it, to one person who has tried to help you: a partner, parent, friend, pastor or colleague. You can add a single line: "This is what helps me." If sending it feels too exposing, save it and mark the one or two of the nine points that matter most to you, so the words are ready for when someone asks. If you are the supporter reading this, choose one small gesture and do it within 24 hours.
reflection_questions: Which of the nine ways would help you most right now? Which one has been missing?
Who has supported you well in the past, perhaps without either of you naming it?
What is one thing you wish the people around you understood about your depression?

scripture.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

days.title: A place to belong this month
days.quote: Indeed, these data suggest that once a person presents with depression it is not "too late" to address their social isolation.
days.quote_source: Cruwys, Dingle, Haslam, Haslam, Jetten & Morton (2013)
days.explanation:
This week has been about noticing, understanding and sending one message. Today is about choosing one group to show up to over the coming month. Not to fix everything. To change the odds, the way the research says group membership does.

What should you look for? Choose a group you could come to feel part of, not one you would merely attend; fit matters more than effort. Choose one with a regular rhythm: in the Korean study, once a week was enough to lower risk. Choose one where you have something to do, however small: a review of 69 trials in older adults found, in a small number of studies, that social activities giving participants an active role reduced depressive symptoms, and that programmes lasting more than three months did better than short ones. And prefer groups over one-to-one befriending, which has generally proved less effective.

The list is wide. A congregation is one option, and a well-studied one: across 444 studies, over 60% found less depression among people active in a faith community, partly because it surrounds them with support. But the English study counted churches alongside music groups, sports clubs, evening classes, residents' groups and charities, and all of them counted. So does a depression support group or group therapy, where everyone in the room knows what this is. If leaving the house is not possible yet, an online group that sometimes meets offline is a bridge. If the first group does not fit, that is information, not failure; in the Australian study about 40% of participants had left their group within three months. Pick one. Go once. Then go again.
days.challenge: Choose one group to show up to this month and take one practical step towards the first visit, within 15 minutes: find the day, time and place, write it in your calendar, and tell one person you are going (perhaps the person you messaged this week). If that is too much, write the name of the group in your journal and nothing else. Naming it is the first step; you can take the second one tomorrow.
reflection_questions: Which group did you choose, and what made you choose it over the others?
What would help you walk through the door the first time: going with someone, arriving early, telling the leader you are new?
A month from now, what would "it went well enough" look like, honestly?

scripture.text: God sets the lonely in families.
